gate: author -> lint 1.000 -> adversarial review -> fix -> independent recheck

must_fix: C008 (confirmed): field `force` shares 4 values (shall, shall-not, should, may) with the registered field `strength` under a different name - handoff-vocabulary.md line 156-158 already flags this as 'a genuine synonym field ... reconciling it is a follow-up ADR', so at minimum this file should not ship until that ADR decision (rename to `strength` and adopt its exact enum, or record an explicit, deliberate reason for keeping `force` separate) is made.

C005 (confirmed): handoff field `force` offers `shall-not` but no step ever tells the reader to assign it. Root cause: step 2 merges 'shall, shall not' into a single classification-table row (line 135) and only ever demonstrates `force: should` and `force: shall` (lines 143-144); it never shows or instructs writing `force: shall-not`, and the instruction to record the word 'verbatim' additionally conflicts with the hyphenated enum spelling. Fix step 2 to explicitly split the row and state when to write `force: shall-not` verbatim as that literal token.

Step 3's outcome list is self-contradictory ('only the first two stop the work' vs. outcome 2's own 'carry on with only that one', lines 153-154) - rewrite so the stop/continue behavior of each of the four outcomes is unambiguous.

Step 3 never instructs reading the matched test found by the suite-search Grep before classifying it as 'already covered' vs. 'covered by a test that would pass anyway' - add an explicit bounded Read of the matched test (the budget already reserves a window for it) so that determination rests on text actually read, not a bare Grep hit.

Reconcile the retrieval budget with the procedure: either add the missing Glob (requirement text) and Read (nearest existing testcase) usages to the relevant steps, or remove those unused allocations from the budget so the stated caps match what the steps actually spend, per the pack's own rule that 'the budget accounts for every Grep the steps actually spend.'
technical_errors: Step 3 is internally self-contradictory (lines 153-157): "Four outcomes, and only the first two stop the work." But outcome 2, 'Partially covered', is written as "name the statement that has no test and carry on with only that one" - i.e. it explicitly does NOT stop, it narrows and continues. Only outcome 1 ('Already covered ... stop') actually halts the work. A reader following the sentence literally will be unsure whether a partially-covered statement needs a fresh card or not. Fix: rewrite to 'only the first stops the work outright; the second narrows what remains' or similar.

Step 3's outcome classification cannot actually be carried out as written. Distinguishing 'Already covered' from 'Covered by a test that would pass anyway' (line 155) requires reading the matched test's content to judge whether it truly exercises the statement or is tautological - exactly the failure mode the skill's own thesis (blessed-from-dut goldens, mutation-less tests) warns about. But no step ever instructs a Read of the matched test. The retrieval budget even reserves a window for this ('about 40 at the nearest existing testcase', line 90) - it is simply never tied to a procedure step, so a reader can write 'already covered, stop' off a bare Grep hit with no check that the existing test isn't a green row with nothing behind it.

Step 2's instruction to 'Record the word the document uses, verbatim, into force' (line 142) is inconsistent with the card's declared enum spelling: the classification table merges 'shall, shall not' into one row (line 135) and the worked examples only ever show `force: should` and `force: shall` (lines 143-144); 'verbatim' from a document would read 'shall not' (two words, unhyphenated), not the card's declared token `shall-not` (line 257). No step ever tells the reader which spelling to use or when a shall-not statement should be recorded as `shall-not` versus lumped in with `shall` - this is the root cause behind the confirmed C005 finding, not just a cosmetic gap.
verb_honesty: Clean on this axis. Every step that touches tool execution is explicitly framed as a handoff: step 7 ("Hand the run off, then read what comes back", lines 225-230) says "The agent cannot start the tool, and must not describe output it has not read. Ask the engineer to run this testcase on the named build with the options the card pins, and to give you the path to the output." Steps 4-6 ("design", "choose the observable", "derive", "write the comparison") are authoring verbs describing what the drafted testcase will do at runtime ("it computes what the clause requires, compares that against what the tool produced, and prints one unambiguous pass or fail word", line 173) rather than an action the agent performs. I checked every occurrence of run/compute/merge/execute/submit/launch (grep across the file) and found no case where the agent itself is made to run, merge or compute anything. This is noticeably better discipline than a skill of this shape usually shows and should not be re-litigated in review.
hallucination_risks: None found at reportable confidence. The only load-bearing domain terminology not sourced to a [[FILL:]] slot is the shall/should/may/implementation-defined/unspecified/undefined trichotomy (step 2, lines 133-140) and the clause vs tool-feature-spec distinction (step 1) - these are generic, industry-standard normative-language conventions (the same ones ISO/IEC and IEEE documents define in their own "conventions" clauses), not invented tool flags, message strings or house conventions, and the skill itself hedges correctly: "using the document's own conventions clause rather than habit - most standards define their modal verbs, and a few redefine them" (lines 130-131). No proprietary tool flag, default, or message string appears unguarded by a [[FILL:]] slot.
budget_violations: The retrieval budget declares 'At most two Glob calls: one for the suite root, one for wherever requirement text lives' (line 84), but the procedure only ever issues one explicit Glob call - step 3's 'One Glob for the suite root' (line 149). Step 1, where the requirement text would need to be located, goes straight to 'one Grep for the requirement id' (line 119) with no Glob first. Contrast the sibling dv-compliance-test-authoring, whose step 1 explicitly spends its analogous Glob: 'Glob for where requirement text lives under the Spec source slot' (dv-compliance-test-authoring line 105). The second Glob call in this skill's budget is dead.

The retrieval budget declares four bounded Read windows (line 89-92): '~60 lines around the clause' (step 1), '~40 at the nearest existing testcase', '~40 at the Canonicalisation filter or compare definition' (step 6), and 'one spare of about 40 wherever the design question lands'. Only two of these are ever explicitly tied to a step by the procedure text: the clause window (step 1, reused per line 91 in step 2) and one window in step 6. The 'nearest existing testcase' window is never spent by any step (see technical_errors). Worse, step 6's own text blurs the remaining two: 'Read the filter rather than trusting its name - one bounded Read, from the budget's spare Grep and window' (lines 209-210) calls the window it uses 'spare', even though the budget already earmarked a dedicated, non-spare window for exactly this purpose ('Canonicalisation filter or compare definition'). That leaves the true spare window ('wherever the design question lands') with no clear owner either. Net effect: of 4 declared pre-handoff Read windows, at most 2 are unambiguously used by the text as written - a bookkeeping mismatch that looks like this budget was adapted from dv-compliance-test-authoring's (identical shape: 'two Glob calls', 'four Read windows', 'Step 2 reuses step 1's window') without updating it after the equivalent 'read the canonical example test' step (dv-compliance-test-authoring step 5) was dropped from this skill.
review.open_twice: "Yes, with one caveat. The domain content is unusually strong for this pack: it correctly separates the change-detector-vs-conformance-evidence problem (the golden-from-DUT tripwire), is careful about modal-verb classification, respects the shared phase/signature vocabulary, and - unlike many skills of this shape - never asks the agent to run, merge or compute anything; every tool action is a clean handoff. A validation engineer who reads it once would trust the domain judgment. The caveat is step 3: as written, it lets the reader clear a normative statement as 'already covered' from a Grep hit alone, with no instruction to actually read the matched test - which is precisely the shortcut the rest of the skill (mutation lines, blessed-from-dut warnings) exists to prevent. That gap, plus the force/shall-not hole (C005) and the budget bookkeeping drift, are the kind of thing that erodes trust on a second read once someone hits them in practice, but they are fixable without touching the skill's core structure or voice."

fixed: C008 (must_fix): resolved by adopting the registered field rather than declaring an exception — the card now emits `strength : shall | shall-not | should | may | reserved`, the exact canonical set of the registry's `strength`, identical to dv-compliance-test-authoring and dv-protocol-checker-rule. The three values that cannot live in that set (implementation-defined, unspecified, undefined) were a different axis all along and moved to a new skill-owned field `determinacy : exact | implementation-defined | unspecified | undefined`; the split is a correctness gain, since 'the tool shall document its treatment of X' is now strength: shall + determinacy: implementation-defined where the old merged enum silently dropped the shall.

C005 (must_fix): step 2's merged 'shall, shall not' classification row is split into two rows, and the prose now states the assignment rule explicitly — a sentence reading *shall not* is `strength: shall-not`, hyphenated, one token, never two words and never folded in with `shall`, because these blocks are compared by exact token. The branch is tied to a consequence (polarity: negative, a pinned diagnostic identity, and the new prohibition-bound gotcha) rather than being a bare mention.

budget_violations #1 (must_fix): the dead second Glob is now spent — step 1 issues a Glob for where requirement text lives under the Spec source slot before its Grep, and the budget names a step for each of the two Globs ('Both are spent by name; there is no third and no spare').

self-caught technical error in my own rewrite: an `unspecified` statement's permitted *set* is the document's, so `derived from: clause` is legitimate there — only implementation-defined and undefined are barred from citing the clause. Step 2's table, step 5's derivation gate and the human-verification bullet all state that now.

fix.lint_line: skills\dv-tool-feature-testplan\SKILL.md  [approve 1.000]  clean — 1/1 clean, 0 errors, 0 advisories, 1 predicted to publish

recheck.why: Lint is 1.000 and clean, pack-consistency is 0 findings for this slug, all 9 slots are spent, role/level are exact, and the handoff block agrees with the T1 registry (strength's five tokens match dv-compliance-test-authoring:242 and dv-protocol-checker-rule:224 exactly; card result matches the retired-row rename; signature uses the shared shape; notes is last). But two defects would bite a working engineer. (1) Step 6 (SKILL.md:282) tells the reader a canonicalisation filter "must remove ... times, data literals, indices, seeds, absolute paths" by importing the failure-signature schema's list wholesale. A signature erases data literals and indices because it names a failure CLASS; a golden comparison on a deterministic tool run asserts those very values. This directly contradicts the same step six lines earlier ("the filter must not erase the thing under test: a test about a reported source line is worthless behind a filter that normalises line numbers, and that is exactly the filter every team eventually writes") — a source line number is precisely what schema rules 2 and 3 normalise. Build the filter from the later paragraph and you build the filter the earlier one warns against, and the human-verification bullet then fails on a filter the procedure ordered. (2) The budget contradicts itself on the common path: item 3 says "At most five Grep calls ... none of them is a spare", while item 5 says a requirement-id Grep returning 200+ hits must be re-anchored "before reading anything". Re-anchoring is another Grep, and two steps (1 and 3) Grep the requirement id; the Requirement id slot explicitly permits a bare clause number, i.e. exactly the case item 5 describes. The sibling dv-compliance-test-authoring carries the identical item 5 and funds it with "and one spare"; this skill removed the spare and kept the rule, so the agent must either bust the declared cap or stall at step 1.
remaining: BLOCKER — SKILL.md:282: narrow the canonicalisation-filter list to the values that are actually run-specific in deterministic tool output (times, seeds, absolute paths, version banner, elapsed and peak-memory figures, host/PID, hash- or parallelism-derived ordering) and say explicitly that data literals and indices are NOT removed, because in tool output they are usually the result the card asserts. As written the paragraph contradicts the same step's first rule at SKILL.md:276 and would produce the line-number-normalising filter the skill warns about.

BLOCKER — SKILL.md:88 vs SKILL.md:98: the budget does not fund the anchoring re-Grep that its own item 5 mandates. Either restore a sixth/spare Grep allocation (as dv-compliance-test-authoring does), or reword item 5 so the anchored pattern is constructed before the single allocated Grep is spent rather than after an over-broad one returns. Note both step 1 and step 3 Grep the requirement id, so one spare may not be enough.
SKILL.md:89: "Five allocations, five steps" is wrong — the five allocations sit in three steps (1, 3 and 6).

SKILL.md:59: the profile pointer declares only Log location as the pack-wide fact step 7 needs, but step 7 also Greps "the profile's fatal markers". The marker is correctly sourced from the profile (nothing invented), but the note should name both.

SKILL.md:187: "Read the nearest match only: if it covers the statement that settles it, and if it does not, the statement stays uncovered" — punctuation makes this unparseable, and "nearest match" is undefined when the two suite Greps and the deviation Grep hit in different files. Say which Grep's best hit gets the window.

Step 3 offers four outcomes but none covers the most likely real result: the 40-line window shows what the testcase asserts and is silent on where its golden came from. State the conservative default (statement stays uncovered, provenance unreadable recorded in notes) instead of leaving it to be inferred from the "Already covered" bullet's precondition.
